** `market_news` reported fetching 119 items (yahoo 49, cnbc 30, marketwatch 10, alpaca 30) and surfaced **15**, and because the cap keeps the *most recent* headlines, all 15 were published in the final 30 minutes before the gather — four of them the identical "12 [Sector] Stocks Moving In Tuesday's After-Market Session" template. The result is that the entire macro narrative of the session was dropped: not one headline about the US–Iran strikes that have crude up 6.55% in five sessions, and consequently `market_events.flags.counts.geopolitical` scored **0** on a night with a ten-day ceasefire proposal live. A required regime input returned a confident false negative, and I only caught it because I ran outside web research. Two cheap fixes: (1) **stratify the headline cap** — reserve half the slots for market-wide/macro stories and half for single-name, instead of sorting purely by recency; (2) **collapse templated Benzinga movers lists** ("N [Sector] Stocks Moving In...") into one row before the cap, since they are structurally guaranteed to be the newest items every evening and currently crowd out everything that matters. Secondary, and cheaper still: nothing in the bundle told me *where* today's money went — `momentum_health` correctly flagged "unwind" but a one-line leadership-rotation read (top and bottom sectors by same-day move) would have handed me the single most important fact of this session instead of my having to reconstruct it from 186 individual `pct_change_1d` fields.

This is adopted lesson LP-8200625986 recurring verbatim, and today it was the *deciding* constraint rather than a nuisance: the scanner should promote the top 2–3 non-focus `top_setups` rows (or any name carrying a >5% 30-day upward EPS revision) into the focus set each run so they receive a chart plus the deep bundle. As it stands, the moment leadership rotates out of my 13 focus names — which is precisely what a momentum unwind *is* — my research depth rotates out with it.

** the watchlist trigger checker is **direction-blind**, and that is what produced this run's false positive. My published PANW condition was a *reclaim* of ~$345 that *holds*; the alert fired because price came within 2% of $345 **from below** (live $340.12, -2.45% on the day) — the opposite of the stated condition. This is the same class of defect as LP-4566902391 (the AMD alert firing 3.9% off the level). Fix: parse a relation token out of `would_buy_at` — "reclaim / above / breaks out / closes above" requires price **at or above** the level, "pullback to / near / dip to / below" requires price **at or below** — and only fire when the relation is satisfied, defaulting to proximity-only with an explicit `relation: unknown` tag when no token parses. Secondary, same block: the alert quoted PANW's stale 7/20 close ($348.66) while `live_prices.json`, written four minutes earlier, carried $340.12 — the alert rows should quote the same live mark the `trigger_run_note` claims to have confirmed on, or the two blocks will keep contradicting each other on exactly the days a trigger matters.

** `momentum_health` was entirely absent from this bundle — no status, no MTUM/SPMO drawdown figures, no signals block — despite CLAUDE.md naming it as a required input to the regime step on *every* run, and this was precisely the week its answer mattered most. I had to infer the factor unwind by hand from `sector_relative_strength` (every AI-stack sector strongly positive on 3m and sharply negative on 1m while SPY was flat), which is a slower and less auditable read than the tool that already exists. Worse, the failure is silent: the fail-open convention treats a missing block as "unknown, no adjustment," which is indistinguishable in the pack from a genuine `unknown` verdict on live data — so on a `weekly_market` depth the gather can drop the block entirely and nothing surfaces it. The fix is small: have the gatherer emit `momentum_health` on every depth (weekly included) and, when it genuinely cannot compute, emit an explicit `{"status": "unavailable", "reason": ...}` stub so the pack distinguishes "the factor is fine" from "nobody looked."

** The deterministic trigger check fired on AMD purely because the *price* touched the parsed $500 level, but my published `would_buy_at` was a compound condition — *post-event* confirmation plus a 50-DMA reclaim, explicitly excluding a pre-event dip. The result is a full event-driven run spun up for a setup that was never actually live, five days before its own catalyst. The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the price alone. That would save event-driven runs for triggers whose *conditions*, not just prices, are met — reducing exactly this kind of "premature trigger" cycle.

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$982 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fund, and would save me from spending the cycle diagnosing broker plumbing instead of setups. Separately, the watchlist trigger checker should parse the *qualitative* half of `would_buy_at` (here, "confirmed positive reaction to the 7/22-23 event... not a bounce off today's low") rather than only the first dollar figure, so it stops firing event-driven runs on price alone before the event has occurred.

** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Secondary: `momentum_health` was absent from this bundle entirely (not even `unknown`), and `position_histories` was `skipped`, so two documented inputs to the regime read were silently missing rather than explicitly null.
